--- title: "Introduction to Numerical Methods in R 🔢" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # Introduction to Numerical Methods in R

Lecture A: floating-point arithmetic, numerical accuracy, series and derivatives

Lecture B: root finding, numerical integration, maximum likelihood, an application

::: notes - Rizzo Chapter 13. Lecture A: computer arithmetic and why "obvious" code fails. Lecture B: the workhorses uniroot, integrate, optimize/mle. ::: # Lecture A: Computer Arithmetic {#part-a} ## Example 13.0: Some Brain Teasers ::: question TRUE or FALSE? ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} 1 == 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 3 - 2 == 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 0.3 - 0.2 == 0.1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 0.4 - 0.2 == 0.2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} 0 == 0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 1 - 1 == 0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 1 - 1 + .1 == .1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 1 + .1 - 1 == .1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} as.integer(2^31 - 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2147483647 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.integer(2^31) # integers are 32-bit ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sprintf("%.20f", 0.1) # 0.1 has no exact binary representation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "0.10000000000000000555" ``` ::: ::: ## Floating-Point Numbers - Doubles (IEEE 754): $\pm(1.b_1b_2\dots b_{52})_2\times 2^{e}$, 53 significant bits $\approx$ 15-16 decimal digits. - **Machine epsilon** $\epsilon = 2^{-52}$: the gap between 1 and the next double. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} .Machine$double.eps; 2^-52 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.22e-16 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.22e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 1 + .Machine$double.eps == 1; 1 + .Machine$double.eps / 2 == 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} .Machine$double.xmax; .Machine$double.xmin ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.798e+308 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.225e-308 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(2^1023 * 2, 2^-1074 / 2) # overflow to Inf, underflow to 0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Inf 0 ``` ::: ::: - Relative error of representing $x$ is at most $\epsilon/2$; errors **accumulate** and are **amplified** by subtraction of nearly equal numbers (catastrophic cancellation). ## Catastrophic Cancellation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) n <- 1000; M <- 2^100 A <- rnorm(n, mean = M, sd = M); B <- rnorm(n, mean = -M, sd = M) c(all_equal = isTRUE(all.equal(A + B - A - B, rep(0, n))), exactly_zero = sum(A + B - A - B == 0), max_abs_error = max(abs(A + B - A - B))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` all_equal exactly_zero max_abs_error 0.000e+00 8.730e+02 5.629e+14 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); boxplot(A - A + B - B, main = "A - A + B - B", horizontal = TRUE) boxplot(A + B - A - B, main = "A + B - A - B", horizontal = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/17-numerical/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Floating-point addition is **not associative**. ## Example: The Sample Variance, Two Ways $$ S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2 \quad\text{vs.}\quad S^2 = \frac{\sum x_i^2 - n\bar x^2}{n-1} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); x <- rnorm(1000, mean = 1e9, sd = 1) # true variance 1 two_pass <- sum((x - mean(x))^2) / (length(x) - 1) one_pass <- (sum(x^2) - length(x) * mean(x)^2) / (length(x) - 1) c(var = var(x), two_pass = two_pass, textbook_one_pass = one_pass) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` var two_pass textbook_one_pass 0.9781 0.9781 0.0000 ``` ::: ::: ::: danger The "computational formula" from intro statistics is numerically unstable. Use two-pass or **Welford's** online algorithm (our R6 example in the OOP lecture). ::: ## Example 13.1: Identical and Nearly Equal ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} isTRUE(all.equal(.2, .3 - .1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} all.equal(.2, .3) # not a logical value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Mean relative difference: 0.5" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} isTRUE(all.equal(.2, .3)) # always a logical value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 1:4; y <- 2 x == y # not necessarily a single logical value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} identical(x, y); identical(y, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: - Use `identical()` in `if`/`while` conditions; `isTRUE(all.equal(...))` for numerical near-equality (tolerance $\approx 1.5\times10^{-8}$). ## Example 13.2: Ratio of Two Large Numbers Evaluate $\dfrac{\Gamma((n-1)/2)}{\Gamma(1/2)\Gamma((n-2)/2)}$ for $n = 400$: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 400 (gamma((n - 1) / 2) / (sqrt(pi) * gamma((n - 2) / 2))) # Inf / Inf ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NaN ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} exp(lgamma((n - 1) / 2) - lgamma((n - 2) / 2)) / sqrt(pi) # work on the log scale ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7.954 ``` ::: ::: ::: tip **Work on the log scale:** `lgamma`, `lchoose`, `lfactorial`, `log1p`, `expm1`, `dnorm(..., log = TRUE)`, `pnorm(..., log.p = TRUE)`, and the **log-sum-exp** trick: $\log\sum e^{a_i} = m + \log\sum e^{a_i - m}$, $m = \max a_i$. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- c(-1000, -1001, -1002) c(naive = log(sum(exp(a))), logsumexp = max(a) + log(sum(exp(a - max(a))))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` naive logsumexp -Inf -999.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(log(1 + 1e-17), log1p(1e-17)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0e+00 1e-17 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 13.3: Taylor Expansion $\sin x = \sum_{k=0}^n\frac{(-1)^k}{(2k+1)!}x^{2k+1}$. Compare a loop with a vectorized polynomial: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- pi / 6; k <- 0:11 c(series = sum((-1)^k * x^(2 * k + 1) / factorial(2 * k + 1)), sin = sin(x)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` series sin 0.5 0.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} system.time(for (i in 1:20000) { # loop s <- 0; for (j in 0:11) s <- s + (-1)^j * x^(2 * j + 1) / factorial(2 * j + 1) }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` user system elapsed 0.128 0.000 0.132 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} system.time(for (i in 1:20000) sum((-1)^k * x^(2 * k + 1) / factorial(2 * k + 1))) # vectorized ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` user system elapsed 0.044 0.000 0.047 ``` ::: ::: ## Series for Large Arguments: Order Matters ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 20 naive <- sum((-1)^(0:60) * x^(2 * (0:60) + 1) / factorial(2 * (0:60) + 1)) reduced <- { xr <- x %% (2 * pi); sum((-1)^(0:30) * xr^(2 * (0:30) + 1) / factorial(2 * (0:30) + 1)) } c(naive = naive, range_reduced = reduced, sin = sin(20)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` naive range_reduced sin 0.9129 0.9129 0.9129 ``` ::: ::: - Terms like $20^{41}/41!$ are huge and alternate in sign: cancellation destroys accuracy. Reduce the argument first. ## Numerical Derivatives (cf. Examples 13.4 - 13.5) Forward difference $\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$ has truncation error $O(h)$ and rounding error $O(\epsilon/h)$: the best $h\approx\sqrt\epsilon$. Central differences: $O(h^2)$, best $h\approx\epsilon^{1/3}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(x) exp(x); x0 <- 1; h <- 10^seq(-16, -1, by = .25) fwd <- abs((f(x0 + h) - f(x0)) / h - exp(1)) ctr <- abs((f(x0 + h) - f(x0 - h)) / (2 * h) - exp(1)) plot(h, fwd, log = "xy", type = "l", lwd = 3, ylab = "absolute error", main = "Truncation vs rounding error") lines(h, ctr, lwd = 3, col = "#C0392B"); abline(v = c(sqrt(.Machine$double.eps), .Machine$double.eps^(1/3)), lty = 2) legend("bottom", c("forward", "central"), col = c(1, "#C0392B"), lwd = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/17-numerical/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Derivative of the Zeta Function (Example 13.5) $\zeta(a) = \sum_{i\ge1}i^{-a}$, $a > 1$, and $\zeta'(a) = -\sum_{i\ge1}\frac{\log i}{i^a}$. Summing the series directly converges slowly; the book uses a Laurent expansion with Stieltjes constants. A simple check: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} zeta <- function(a, N = 1e6) { i <- 1:N; sum(i^-a) + N^(1 - a) / (a - 1) } # tail correction dzeta_series <- function(a, N = 1e6) { i <- 1:N; -sum(log(i) * i^-a) - N^(1 - a) * (log(N) / (a - 1) + 1 / (a - 1)^2) } a <- 2; h <- 1e-4 c(series = dzeta_series(a), central_difference = (zeta(a + h) - zeta(a - h)) / (2 * h), known = -0.9375482543) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` series central_difference known -0.9375 -0.9375 -0.9375 ``` ::: ::: # Lecture B: Root Finding, Integration, MLE {#part-b} ## Root Finding: Bisection If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $f(a)f(b) < 0$, a root lies in $(a,b)$. Halve the interval each step: error after $k$ steps $\le (b-a)/2^k$ (linear convergence). **Example 13.6.** Solve $a^2 + y^2 + \dfrac{2ay}{n-1} = n-2$ for $y$, with $a = 0.5$, $n = 20$. Exact: $y = -\dfrac{a}{n-1}\pm\sqrt{n-2-a^2+\left(\dfrac{a}{n-1}\right)^2}$ (the 2nd edition prints $+a^2$ under the root, a typo). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(y, a, n) a^2 + y^2 + 2 * a * y / (n - 1) - (n - 2) a <- 0.5; n <- 20 b0 <- 0; b1 <- 5* n; it <- 0; eps <- .Machine$double.eps^0.25 y <- seq(b0, b1, length = 100) r <- c(b0, b1); f0 <- f(b0, a, n); f1 <- f(b1, a, n) while (it < 1000 && abs(r[2] - r[1]) > eps) { it <- it + 1; mid <- mean(r); fm <- f(mid, a, n) if (fm == 0) { r <- c(mid, mid); break } if (f0 * fm < 0) { r[2] <- mid; f1 <- fm } else { r[1] <- mid; f0 <- fm } } c(root = mean(r), iterations = it, exact = -a / (n - 1) + sqrt(n - 2 - a^2 + (a / (n - 1))^2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` root iterations exact 4.187 20.000 4.187 ``` ::: ::: ## Example 13.7: Brent's Method with `uniroot` Brent's method combines bisection, the secant method, and inverse quadratic interpolation: guaranteed and fast. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} out <- uniroot(function(y) f(y, a, n), lower = 0, upper = 5 * n) unlist(out[c("root", "f.root", "iter", "estim.prec")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` root f.root iter estim.prec 4.187e+00 2.381e-04 1.400e+01 6.104e-05 ``` ::: ::: **Newton-Raphson:** $x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k)$, quadratic convergence near the root but no guarantee. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} newton <- function(f, df, x, tol = 1e-12, maxit = 50) { for (k in 1:maxit) { step <- f(x) / df(x); x <- x - step; if (abs(step) < tol) break } c(root = x, iterations = k) } newton(function(y) f(y, a, n), function(y) 2 * y + 2 * a / (n - 1), x = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` root iterations 4.187 7.000 ``` ::: ::: ## Numerical Integration: `integrate()` Adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature (QUADPACK). Handles infinite limits by transformation. **Example 13.8.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} integrate(dnorm, -1.96, 1.96) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.95 with absolute error < 1e-11 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} integrate(dnorm, -Inf, Inf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 with absolute error < 9.4e-05 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} integrate(function(y) exp(-y^2 / 2) / sqrt(2 * pi), 0, Inf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.5 with absolute error < 4.7e-05 ``` ::: ::: ::: danger `integrate` must receive a **vectorized** integrand, and can be fooled by narrow peaks: `integrate(dnorm, 0, 20000)` claims about 0! ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} integrate(dnorm, 0, 20000)$value; integrate(dnorm, 0, Inf)$value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5 ``` ::: ::: ## Quadrature by Hand: Trapezoid and Simpson ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} trap <- function(f, a, b, m) { x <- seq(a, b, length = m + 1); h <- (b - a) / m; h * (sum(f(x)) - (f(a) + f(b)) / 2) } simpson <- function(f, a, b, m) { # m even x <- seq(a, b, length = m + 1); h <- (b - a) / m h / 3 * (f(a) + f(b) + 4 * sum(f(x[seq(2, m, 2)])) + 2 * sum(f(x[seq(3, m - 1, 2)]))) } g <- function(x) exp(-x) / (1 + x^2); exact <- integrate(g, 0, 1, rel.tol = 1e-12)$value sapply(c(4, 16, 64), function(m) c(m = m, trapezoid_err = trap(g, 0, 1, m) - exact, simpson_err = simpson(g, 0, 1, m) - exact)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] m 4.0000000 1.600e+01 6.400e+01 trapezoid_err 0.0033273 2.059e-04 1.286e-05 simpson_err -0.0001636 -5.374e-07 -2.083e-09 ``` ::: ::: - Errors $O(m^{-2})$ (trapezoid) and $O(m^{-4})$ (Simpson) in 1-d, versus $O(m^{-1/2})$ for Monte Carlo (Ch 6), but quadrature degrades quickly in higher dimensions. ## Example 13.9: Density of the Sample Correlation For bivariate normal data with correlation $\rho$, the density of $r$ is $$ f(r) = \frac{(n-2)(1-\rho^2)^{(n-1)/2}(1-r^2)^{(n-4)/2}}{\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{dw}{(\cosh w - \rho r)^{n-1}},\quad -1 1 || abs(rho) > 1) return(0) if (N < 4) return(NA) if (isTRUE(all.equal(rho, 0.0))) { a <- exp(lgamma((N - 1) / 2) - lgamma((N - 2) / 2)) return(a * (1 - r^2)^((N - 4) / 2) / sqrt(pi)) } f <- function(w, R, N, rho) (cosh(w) - rho * R)^(1 - N) # integrand i <- integrate(f, lower = 0, upper = Inf, R = r, N = N, rho = rho)$value c1 <- (N - 2) * (1 - rho^2)^((N - 1) / 2) c2 <- (1 - r^2)^((N - 4) / 2) / pi c1 * c2 * i } dcorr <- function(r, N, rho = 0) sapply(r, .dcorr, N = N, rho = rho) integrate(dcorr, -1, 1, N = 10, rho = 0.5)$value # a proper density? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Checking the Density by Simulation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); N <- 10; rho <- 0.5 rs <- replicate(20000, cor(MASS::mvrnorm(N, c(0, 0), matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2)))[1, 2]) hist(rs, prob = TRUE, breaks = 60, col = "#FFCC00", main = "Sample correlation, n = 10, rho = 0.5", xlab = "r") curve(dcorr(x, N = N, rho = rho), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "#003366", n = 200) curve(dcorr(x, N = N, rho = 0), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2, n = 200) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/17-numerical/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Maximum Likelihood Problems (Example 13.10) $Y_1, Y_2\iid\text{Exp}(\theta)$: $\ell(\theta) = 2\log\theta - \theta(y_1+y_2)$, $\hat\theta = 2/(y_1+y_2)$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(0.04304550, 0.50263474) mlogL <- function(theta = 1) -(length(y) * log(theta) - theta * sum(y)) # minus log-likelihood library(stats4) fit <- mle(mlogL) summary(fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Maximum likelihood estimation Call: mle(minuslogl = mlogL) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error theta 3.665 2.592 -2 log L: -1.195 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(closed_form = 2 / sum(y)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` closed_form 3.665 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} optimize(mlogL, lower = 0.01, upper = 50)$minimum # 1-d alternative ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.665 ``` ::: ::: ## Application: Evaluating an Expected Value (Examples 13.11 - 13.13) $X\sim\text{Pareto}(\sigma, \alpha = 1)$, $\bar F(x) = (\sigma/x)^\alpha$, $x\ge\sigma$. For $y>\sigma$ and $0<\beta<1$, evaluate $\E|y - X|^\beta$ (it arises in energy goodness-of-fit tests). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} f1 <- function(x, y, s, a, b) (abs(y - x))^b * a * s^a / x^(a + 1) # the integrand |y-x|^b f(x) g1 <- function(y, s, a, b) { # E|y-X|^b by numerical integration if (y < s) return(NA) integrate(f1, lower = s, upper = y, y = y, s = s, a = a, b = b)$value + integrate(f1, lower = y, upper = Inf, y = y, s = s, a = a, b = b)$value } sapply(c(1.5, 2, 5, 10), g1, s = 1, a = 1, b = .5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.452 1.487 2.057 2.922 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); X <- 1 / runif(1e6) # Pareto(1, 1) by inverse transform sapply(c(1.5, 2, 5, 10), function(y) mean(abs(y - X)^.5)) # Monte Carlo check ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.446 1.481 2.050 2.915 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - The book also derives a closed form as an infinite series (hypergeometric functions, VGAM/gsl) and compares it with integrate; the plot of E|y - X|^b versus y is Example 13.13. ::: ## Example 13.13: The Expected Distance Function ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ys <- seq(1.01, 20, length = 100) plot(ys, sapply(ys, g1, s = 1, a = 1, b = .5), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#003366", xlab = "y", ylab = expression(E * "|" * y - X * "|"^beta), main = "Pareto(1, 1), beta = 0.5") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/17-numerical/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - Doubles have about 16 significant digits; avoid `==` (use `isTRUE(all.equal())`), avoid subtracting nearly equal numbers, work on the log scale. - Derivatives: step size $\sqrt\epsilon$ (forward) or $\epsilon^{1/3}$ (central). - Roots: bisection (safe), Newton (fast), Brent's `uniroot` (both). - Integrals: `integrate()` (vectorize the integrand, beware of peaks), trapezoid/Simpson, Monte Carlo in high dimensions. - MLE: `optimize()` (1-d), `stats4::mle()`, `optim()` (next lecture). :::
